I am 50 years old this year, and I have been farming my family's land in Quzhou since I was a teenager. I never went to school, but I know this land and this climate with my hands and my eyes. We have about 8 mu of good flat land here on the North China Plain, and everyone in my village does the same rotation: winter wheat followed by summer maize. That is what the land and the water allow.

For the wheat, I will sow my own saved seed this autumn — I have kept good seed from last year's harvest, cleaned it, and that has always worked for me. Before sowing, I will run the rotary tiller to prepare the seedbed. I will put down one bag of compound fertilizer as basal dressing, and then after the winter, when the wheat wakes up in spring, I will topdress with urea at jointing. I will irrigate four times: the winter irrigation to protect from freezing, then again at green-up, at heading, and once more during grain filling if the sky does not give us rain. I usually spray pesticides about four times — mainly for aphids and fungus when the weather turns humid.

After harvesting the wheat in early June, I will immediately plant summer maize. For maize I always buy hybrid seed from the shop — I usually get Denghai or Nongda varieties because the shopkeeper says they are good and I have seen they yield better and handle the weather well. I will not till again for the maize; I will direct-seed into the wheat stubble to save time and fuel, before the soil dries out. Maize needs less irrigation than wheat because the summer rains come, but I will water at least twice — once right after sowing to get it up, and once at the big flare stage if the rains fail. I will spray for pests three times, especially for corn borers. I expect about 1000 jin per mu of wheat and a bit more from the maize if the weather is fair.
